A printed cabinet of the Scribe’s historic, magical and imagined writing hands, set beside the familiar letters of English.

Every sheet preserves the Scribe’s own letter mappings and description, with its original feather artwork. The hand-written passage below each English description is a transcription of English in the selected writing system, unless a native-language vocabulary specimen is explicitly identified.

Ancient scripts and undeciphered symbols are not automatically English A–Z alphabets. The printed keys show exactly how the current Scribe types them. The original vocabulary specimens are drawn from its own language packs.

The hidden hands

Theban

❧MAGICAL CIPHER❧
SECTION IThe Origins of the Script
ORIGINRenaissance Europe · early 1500s
PURPOSEMagical writing, inscriptions and concealed text
DIRECTIONLeft → Right

A secret hand from the old occult books, its letters dressed in unfamiliar shapes so ordinary words could travel beneath another face. Often called the Witches’ Alphabet, Theban changes the writing, not the language.

An old magician’s alphabet passed down through Renaissance books of hidden learning. Despite its grand name, this is not the lost speech of ancient Chaldea, but a ciphered hand for words already known.

Elder Futhark

❧HISTORICAL SCRIPT❧
SECTION IThe Origins of the Script
ORIGINEarly Germanic Europe
PURPOSENames, marks, memorials and inscriptions
DIRECTIONLeft → Right · Greenman default

Twenty-four runes cut for an older Germanic world, made for wood, bone, metal and stone rather than the smooth page. Greenman can set modern English into these ancient runes, but beneath the runes the language remains English.

Old English / Anglo-Saxon Futhorc

❧HISTORICAL SCRIPT❧
SECTION IThe Origins of the Script
ORIGINAnglo-Saxon England and Frisia · approximately 5th–11th centuries
PURPOSEModern-English rune transcription
DIRECTIONLeft → Right

The expanded rune-row used in Anglo-Saxon England and Frisia. Type any English words and Greenman writes them in this Futhorc hand. This changes the writing system, not the language itself.

Runes & ancient marks

Ogham

❧HISTORICAL SCRIPT❧
SECTION IThe Origins of the Script
ORIGINEarly medieval Ireland and western Britain
PURPOSENames, memorial stones and territorial marks
DIRECTIONBottom → Top · Greenman stave presentation

Lines and notches climbing the edge of stone, carrying names through the rain of Ireland and western Britain. Ogham belongs to the earliest written forms of Irish, though modern words may also be carefully transcribed into its strokes.

Runes & ancient marks

Pictish Symbols

❧UNDECIPHERED❧
SECTION IThe Origins of the Script
ORIGINEarly medieval Scotland
PURPOSEHistorical symbol inscriptions · exact meaning uncertain
DIRECTIONReference / catalogue

Beasts, crescents, mirrors and strange paired signs left across the stones of Pictland. Their makers clearly meant something by them, but that meaning has not yet returned to us. Greenman may recognise and name the symbols, but will never pretend to translate what no one can securely read.

Tengwar

❧CONSTRUCTED SCRIPT❧
SECTION IThe Origins of the Script
ORIGINJ. R. R. Tolkien’s legendarium
PURPOSEQuenya, Sindarin, English and other named modes
DIRECTIONLeft → Right

Tolkien’s flowing letters, elegant enough to look sung rather than written. Tengwar is a writing system with different modes, so its letters change their duties according to the language being written.

The ancient languages

Ugaritic

❧GENUINE LANGUAGE❧
SECTION IThe Origins of the Script
ORIGINLate Bronze Age Ugarit · Syrian coast
PURPOSEReligious, literary, administrative and everyday texts
DIRECTIONLeft → Right

Letters pressed into clay more than three thousand years ago on the Syrian coast. These wedge-shaped signs carried a real language through hymns, myths, letters and records. Here the Scribe can step beyond disguising English and into a controlled piece of Ugaritic itself.

The ancient languages

Hieratic

❧GENUINE LANGUAGE · SCRIPT❧
SECTION IThe Origins of the Script
ORIGINAncient Egypt
PURPOSELetters, accounts, stories, prayers and scribal records
DIRECTIONRight → Left · usual Greenman presentation

The pen-hand of ancient Egypt, where the monumental shapes of hieroglyphs loosened into quicker strokes across papyrus. Scribes used Hieratic for letters, accounts, stories, prayers and the ordinary business of a civilisation.

Hebrew

SECTION IThe Origins of the Script
ORIGINAncient Near Eastern tradition to the present
PURPOSEReligious, literary and modern everyday Hebrew

A right-to-left script carrying a very long trail of sacred writing, scholarship, poetry and everyday speech. Greenman keeps modern Hebrew translation separate from older Biblical forms, so one age is never quietly passed off as another.
